metadata.section: onenmt v3b — indic multilingual neural machine translation
metadata.text:
OneNMT v3b is a **1.1B parameter** multilingual seq2seq translation model supporting **36 × 36 language pairs** across 35 Indian languages and English. It is based on a deep `transformer_18_18` architecture (18 encoder + 18 decoder layers) trained with fairseq and converted to the HuggingFace MBart format.

> ⚠️ **Tokenization Warning:** OneNMT v3b uses a custom fairseq dictionary (`fairseq_dict.json`) for token ID mapping. Using `AutoTokenizer` or any standard MBart tokenizer will produce wrong IDs and garbled output. Always use the provided `hf_inference.py` or the `translate_onemt()` wrapper.

---

**"श्रुतम्" (Shrutam) = "that which is heard"** — a multilingual **11 Indic languages → English** neural machine translation model, built as a **Transformer trained completely from scratch** (no pretrained weights, no fine-tuning shortcuts) on the AI4Bharat Samanantar parallel corpus.

Supports: Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu → English, all in a **single shared model**.

This is a from-first-principles implementation of the original *"Attention Is All You Need"* (Vaswani et al., 2017) transformer architecture — encoder, decoder, multi-head attention, positional encodings, label smoothing, Noam learning-rate schedule, beam search — all hand-written in PyTorch, scaled up and extended for multilingual training.

Indic Translate

---

What is Indic Translate?

**A translation model for English and 22 Indian languages, built for document-length text.**

Indic Translate translates between English and all 22 languages of the Eighth Schedule of the
Indian Constitution, in both directions. It is a single-purpose translation model: it
takes one instruction and one piece of source text, and returns the translation. Nothing
else.

Unlike sentence-level MT systems, Indic Translate is designed to take a **whole document in one
request**, up to 32,768 tokens, and return a translation that preserves the document's
paragraph structure, headings, lists, and inline markup.

This release adds three new capabilities: translating directly to and from **Romanized**
script (writing an Indic language with Latin letters, the way people commonly type without
an Indic keyboard), **transliteration**, converting between native and Romanized script
without changing the language, and **code-mixed** translation, to and from text that mixes
English and an Indic language within a sentence.

A conversational/casual-register domain adaptation of
`ai4bharat/indictrans2-en-indic-1B`,
produced with **experience replay** (mixed fine-tuning) + **model souping** (WiSE-FT-style
weight averaging with the base, α=0.6).

> **Scope of the claim — please read.** On the **chrF2** metric, this model **beats
> IndicTrans2-1B on conversational test sets across all 21 Indic languages** (mean **+6.2**,
> paired-bootstrap significant, p ≤ 0.004 on the hardest subtitle tests) while **matching**
> the base on general-domain **FLORES** (mean change −0.17, all within ±0.7 chrF).
> This is a **chrF result**, not a verified human-quality improvement: part of the conversational
> gain plausibly reflects *style-matching* to casual subtitle references rather than better
> adequacy, and a controlled human evaluation has **not** yet confirmed a perceived quality gain.
> Use accordingly. See the paper for the full, honest evaluation and limitations.

VAGMI translates on-device with NLLB-200, which is CC-BY-NC and therefore cannot ship in a commercial product. Dhee-Vagmi-Core removes that block by being OURS: a ~301M M2M100-architecture model trained from scratch on open, commercially-usable parallel data, covering 20 languages in all 380 directions.

v3 shipped an English-PIVOT model and the distinction is the whole point: an English-centric corpus only ever teaches 2(n-1) directions, so v3 learned 22 of a possible 132 and reached the rest, badly, zero-shot. v4 is trained on explicit non-English pairs -- 11.9M gold Indic<->Indic sentence pairs recovered by joining two Samanantar rows through their shared English, plus a machine-translated block that carries the 8 world languages -- so every direction it claims is a direction it saw.

It is deliberately the same architecture and FLORES-200 tagging VAGMI's on-device ONNX translator already uses, so shipping it is a model swap, not a pipeline rewrite. Deep encoder / shallow decoder keeps decode latency low on a phone.

What this model is NOT for: it is not a general LLM and not a document summariser. Sentence/short-passage translation across its 20 languages is the whole job; widening the remit would trade away the size and latency that make it shippable.

1. QUALITY. chrF++ macro-averaged over ALL 380 directions -- an unweighted mean, so a data-starved direction cannot hide behind a well-resourced one -- within reach of NLLB-200-distilled-600M, the model it replaces. Non-English directions are held to the same bar as English ones from v4 on: they are trained explicitly now, not reached zero-shot, so a weak Tamil<->Bengali is a result and no longer an excuse.

2. LICENCE. Every training corpus must be commercially usable (Samanantar is CC-BY). A single CC-BY-NC or GPL source contaminates the point of the model and fails the run regardless of the score.

3. ON-DEVICE. Exports to INT8 ONNX and runs under onnxruntime-mobile at a size comparable to the current NLLB bundle. A checkpoint that scores well but will not quantise/export is not shippable and has not succeeded.

We use the **MILPaC** **(Multilingual Indian Legal Parallel Corpus)** corpus for fine-tuning. It is the first high-quality Indian legal parallel corpus, containing parallel aligned text units in English (EN) and nine Indian (IN) languages -- Bengali (BN), Hindi (HI), Marathi (MR), Tamil (TA), Telugu (TE), Malayalam (ML), Panjabi (PA), Gujarati (GU), and Oriya (OR). Please refer to the paper for more details about this corpus.

For fine-tuning, we randomly split MILPaC language-wise in a 80 (train) - 10 (validation) - 10 (test) ratio. We use the 80\% train split (combined 80\% of each English-to-Indic language pair) to fine-tune the IndicTrans2 model and 10\% validation split (combined 10\% of each English-to-Indic language pair) to select the best checkpoint and to prevent overfitting.

Hy-MT2-1.8B is Tencent Hunyuan's translation model: it translates between 33
languages and takes terminology, background information and earlier lines in
its prompt. At 1.8B parameters it is fast enough to translate live captions as
they are spoken.

The package was built with the onnxruntime-genai model builder:

- Weight-only INT4 (`MatMulNBits`, round-to-nearest), activations FP16.
- `GroupQueryAttention` over a KV cache shared between past and present, so a
  runtime can keep the cache of the previous request and only prefill what
  follows the shared prefix.
- The LM head is computed for the last position only (`prune_lm_head`).
- The builder's `model.onnx` is published as `model_int4.onnx` (its weights as
  `model_int4.onnx.data`); `genai_config.json` names it.
- One fix to make the builder run: it reads `rope_theta` from the model config,
  which Hy-MT2 keeps under `rope_parameters`. A wrapper set `rope_theta` from
  there before building. The graph itself is the builder's.

What is Indic Translate?

**A translation model for English and 22 Indian languages, built for document-length text.**

Indic Translate translates between English and all 22 languages of the Eighth Schedule of the
Indian Constitution, in both directions. It is a single-purpose translation model: it
takes one instruction and one piece of source text, and returns the translation. Nothing
else.

Unlike sentence-level MT systems, Indic Translate is designed to take a **whole document in one
request**, up to 32,768 tokens, and return a translation that preserves the document's
paragraph structure, headings, lists, and inline markup.

This release adds three new capabilities: translating directly to and from **Romanized**
script (writing an Indic language with Latin letters, the way people commonly type without
an Indic keyboard), **transliteration**, converting between native and Romanized script
without changing the language, and **code-mixed** translation, to and from text that mixes
English and an Indic language within a sentence.

Dhee-Vagmi-Core removes that block by being OURS: a ~301M M2M100-architecture model trained from scratch on open, commercially-usable parallel data, covering 20 languages in all 380 directions.

An ONNX export of ai4bharat/indictrans2-en-indic-dist-200M
by AI4Bharat (IIT Madras), MIT licence, for on-device use with ONNX Runtime
(Android). Weights are dynamically quantized to int8.

All credit for the model goes to AI4Bharat:

> Gala et al., *IndicTrans2: Towards High-Quality and Accessible Machine
> Translation Models for all 22 Scheduled Indian Languages*, TMLR 2023.

- `encoder.onnx`: `input_ids`, `attention_mask` → `hidden`, each decoder
  layer's cross-attention keys and values (`cross_k_i`, `cross_v_i`), and
  `empty_cache`, an empty self-attention cache for the first step.
- `decoder.onnx`: one token per step with a self-attention cache:
  `input_ids`, `encoder_hidden_states`, `encoder_attention_mask`,
  `self_k_i`, `self_v_i`, `cross_k_i`, `cross_v_i` → `logits`,
  `present_k_i`, `present_v_i`.
- `vocab.json`: the source SentencePiece pieces and dictionary, the target
  dictionary, and the model's special token ids and sizes.

The input is prepared as AI4Bharat's IndicProcessor does
(`eng_Latn hin_Deva `); the output is Devanagari for
all targets, transliterated to the target script afterwards (e.g. Gujarati).

Checked against the original PyTorch model: the same greedy translations on
test sentences in Hindi, Marathi and Gujarati.

A conversational/casual-register domain adaptation of
`ai4bharat/indictrans2-en-indic-1B`,
produced with **experience replay** (mixed fine-tuning) + **model souping** (WiSE-FT-style
weight averaging with the base, α=0.6).

> **Scope of the claim — please read.** On the **chrF2** metric, this model **beats
> IndicTrans2-1B on conversational test sets across all 21 Indic languages** (mean **+6.2**,
> paired-bootstrap significant, p ≤ 0.004 on the hardest subtitle tests) while **matching**
> the base on general-domain **FLORES** (mean change −0.17, all within ±0.7 chrF).
> This is a **chrF result**, not a verified human-quality improvement: part of the conversational
> gain plausibly reflects *style-matching* to casual subtitle references rather than better
> adequacy, and a controlled human evaluation has **not** yet confirmed a perceived quality gain.
> Use accordingly. See the paper for the full, honest evaluation and limitations.

- **Use for:** English → Indic translation of **casual / conversational** text (chat, dialogue, subtitles).
- **Direction:** English → Indic only. Indic → English / Indic ↔ Indic are untested.
- **Register:** tuned toward casual register; for formal/news text the base model is at least as good.

- **Low-resource ceiling:** very low-resource languages (e.g. Santali, Sanskrit, Kashmiri) remain
  bounded by the base model's absolute quality.

| Lang | conv | FLORES |
|---|---|---|
| Hindi | 53.9 → 56.8 (+2.9) | 60.0 → 59.6 |
| Tamil | 52.7 → 55.1 (+2.4) | 64.1 → 64.4 |
| Bengali | 68.7 → 73.6 (+4.8) | 58.1 → 58.1 |
| Malayalam | 45.7 → 48.4 (+2.7) | 61.1 → 61.4 |
| Marathi | 70.2 → 77.3 (+7.1) | 55.0 → 54.5 |
| **mean (21 langs)** | **+6.2** | **−0.17** |

meta.text:
OneNMT v3b is a **1.1B parameter** multilingual seq2seq translation model supporting **36 × 36 language pairs** across 35 Indian languages and English. It is based on a deep `transformer_18_18` architecture (18 encoder + 18 decoder layers) trained with fairseq and converted to the HuggingFace MBart format.

> ⚠️ **Tokenization Warning:** OneNMT v3b uses a custom fairseq dictionary (`fairseq_dict.json`) for token ID mapping. Using `AutoTokenizer` or any standard MBart tokenizer will produce wrong IDs and garbled output. Always use the provided `hf_inference.py` or the `translate_onemt()` wrapper.

metadata.text: This is the model card of ***InLegalTrans-En2Indic-1B*** translation model, a fine-tuned version of the IndicTrans2 model specifically tailored for translating Indian legal texts from English to Indian languages.

The following table contains the performance results of the InLegalTrans model compared to the IndicTrans2 model over the 10\% test split of **MILPaC**. Performances are evaluated using *BLEU*, *GLEU*, and *chrF++* metrics. For all English-to-Indic language pairs, InLegalTrans demonstrated a significant improvement over IndicTrans2, achieving consistently better performance across all evaluation metrics.

We use the **MILPaC** **(Multilingual Indian Legal Parallel Corpus)** corpus for fine-tuning. It is the first high-quality Indian legal parallel corpus, containing parallel aligned text units in English (EN) and nine Indian (IN) languages -- Bengali (BN), Hindi (HI), Marathi (MR), Tamil (TA), Telugu (TE), Malayalam (ML), Panjabi (PA), Gujarati (GU), and Oriya (OR). Please refer to the paper for more details about this corpus.

For fine-tuning, we randomly split MILPaC language-wise in a 80 (train) - 10 (validation) - 10 (test) ratio. We use the 80\% train split (combined 80\% of each English-to-Indic language pair) to fine-tune the IndicTrans2 model and 10\% validation split (combined 10\% of each English-to-Indic language pair) to select the best checkpoint and to prevent overfitting.
